extracted.intended_audience: philosophers of mathematics, mathematicians interested in mathematical practice, and researchers working on AI-generated proofs
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating or producing mathematical proofs according to whether a reader can rationally reconstruct the prover's plan (goals, sub-goals, strategies, tactics, and avoided failure points). Applies to assessing readers' understanding, human-written expositions, and auto-generated proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding as plan reconstruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding a proof = rationally reconstructing the underlying plan that the prover executed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reader understands when they can recover the plan from the linear text. This is the central criterion: surface-level syntactic checking is not understanding unless the plan is recoverable. The reconstruction must be rational (see the Rationality Constraint entry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan: partial mental representation organizing activity
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof plan is a partial mental representation that organizes activity over time (Bratman background).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret proofs as embodying partial plans rather than complete scripts; evaluate whether exposition makes this partial structure recoverable (i.e., leaves out irrelevant details while organizing key aims and means).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hierarchical structure of plans
rubrics_metrics.description: Plans have a hierarchical structure: goals, sub-goals, means, and sub-means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the exposition makes the hierarchy explicit or recoverable (e.g., theorem → lemmas → constructions → calculations). Lack of visible hierarchy makes plan-recovery harder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stability and revisability of plans
rubrics_metrics.description: Plans are stable (resist revision without reason) yet revisable when new information appears.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the proof exposition indicates which parts of the plan are essential/stable and which are contingent/revisable (helpful for readers who may need to adapt or generalize the argument).

rubrics_metrics.name: Plans support coordination with others/readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Plans support coordination with other agents (collaborators, future readers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good expositions facilitate coordination: they enable others to continue, check, or modify the argument. Assess whether the text signals project structure and interaction points for readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall goal identification
rubrics_metrics.description: The reader must identify the overall goal (the theorem statement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the top-level element of the plan; check that the exposition foregrounds the target result and frames subsequent steps in relation to it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major sub-goals identification
rubrics_metrics.description: The reader must identify major sub-goals (the lemmas, the cases, the constructions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the exposition names or makes apparent the lemmas/cases and how they decompose the overall goal. Unnamed or stealth sub-goals impede plan reconstruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategy linking sub-goals to the goal
rubrics_metrics.description: The reader must identify the strategy linking sub-goals to the goal (e.g., 'we will reduce to the compact case, then use Stone–Weierstrass').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the exposition states or implies an overarching strategy or merely strings together steps. Explicit strategy statements strongly support understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tactical choices at sub-goals
rubrics_metrics.description: The reader must identify tactical choices at each sub-goal (e.g., 'we induct on n because the statement is dimension-stable').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good exposition justifies why particular tactics are chosen at particular points. Absence of tactical justification makes steps feel arbitrary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure points avoided
rubrics_metrics.description: The reader must recognize failure points that were avoided and understand why a route was chosen because obvious alternatives don't work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expositions that acknowledge and explain rejected approaches (or why simple attempts fail) help readers see why the given plan is rational and necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of each step in advancing the plan
rubrics_metrics.description: The reader must see the role of each step in advancing the plan (no decorative steps).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether each computation or lemma is tied back to the plan-level goals; steps presented without connection obstruct understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graded/partial understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding is graded: readers can have no plan reconstruction, partial plan, full plan without modifiability, or a modifiable plan that supports adaptation to variants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a graduated rubric to place readers or expositions along this continuum. Scoring guidance: identify whether only top-level goals, some sub-strategies, or full modifiable plans are recoverable; higher scores require modifiability and capacity to adapt the plan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationality constraint
rubrics_metrics.description: The plan must be rationally reconstructed — the reader must see why each choice was made, not just what was done.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish mere procedural memorization from genuine understanding. A justification of choices (including alternatives rejected) is required for rational reconstruction. Anti-patterns: memorizing steps, following a script without grasping alternatives, recognizing steps without integration into a plan.

rubrics_metrics.name: State the strategy up-front in exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof exposition supports plan-recovery when it states the strategy at the top (e.g., 'the proof proceeds in three stages').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scoring note: presence of an explicit roadmap/overview is a major positive indicator. Examples: introductory paragraph outlining stages. Anti-pattern: hiding the strategy and proceeding step-by-step with no overview.

rubrics_metrics.name: Name sub-goals as they arise
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof exposition supports plan-recovery when it names sub-goals as they arise (e.g., 'we now establish the key lemma that...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether lemmas and cases are signposted and explained in terms of their contribution to the main goal. Unsignposted lemmas function as 'deus ex machina' and are penalized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify tactical choices
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof exposition supports plan-recovery when it justifies tactical choices (e.g., 'we induct on n rather than m because...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the text explains why a particular tactic was chosen over alternatives; unexplained tactics reduce recoverability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge abandoned or failed routes
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof exposition supports plan-recovery when it acknowledges abandoned routes (e.g., 'the obvious approach via X fails because...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly stating why certain natural approaches are discarded helps readers understand the constraints shaping the plan. This is strong evidence of rational reconstruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connect each step to its role in the plan
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof exposition supports plan-recovery when it connects each step to its role in the plan, not as an isolated computation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether calculations and technical lemmas are followed by commentary tying them to sub-goals or strategies. Anti-patterns: mixing plan-level and tactical-level reasoning without hierarchy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obstructive exposition patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain exposition patterns obstruct plan-recovery: hiding the strategy, concealing motivations, treating sub-goals as deus ex machina, and mixing plan-level and tactical-level reasoning at the same level of detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a proof, mark down these anti-patterns. They indicate that, even if formally correct, the exposition impedes understanding. Use them as negative scoring items or comments for revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess AI/auto-generated proofs for presence of a plan
rubrics_metrics.description: Auto-generated proofs may be logically correct and syntactically well-formed yet unintelligible if no plan was ever formulated; evaluate whether the system produced or can present a plan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For machine-generated proofs, require evidence of an explicit plan (overview, sub-goals, tactic justification, avoided routes) in addition to formal verification. Scoring should penalize proofs that pass formal checks but fail the plan-reconstruction test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation to abilities- and dialectic-based frameworks
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding-as-plan-reconstruction is complementary to Avigad's abilities-based account (what readers can do) and to Lakatos's dialectic (how the plan developed historically vs. as presented).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In evaluation, consider whether an exposition supports downstream abilities (e.g., applying results, modifying proofs) and whether it communicates dialectical development when helpful. This can be used as secondary scoring: plan-recovery that also enables abilities and shows development is highest-quality.
